analysis.one_liner: Phases out giant factory farms, makes meat companies liable for farm pollution, and restores country-of-origin meat labels.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with five Senate backers in February 2023, never received a committee hearing or vote and died when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have stopped new large factory farms, forced existing ones to shut down by 2041, and paid owners up to $10 billion a year to retire their debt and switch to other farming. It would have made meat companies that control contract farms legally responsible for pollution and harms to neighbors, required large packers to buy at least half their livestock through open competitive bidding, and restored "Product of USA" and country-of-origin labels on beef, pork, and dairy. The Senate Agriculture Committee never acted on it, and it expired when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Independent livestock producers and contract poultry and hog growers, who would get stronger rights and open-market prices for their animals; rural residents living near large factory farms, who would get relief from manure, odors, and water contamination; small and mid-size farms competing against operations backed by deep-pocketed meat companies; and shoppers, who would know where their meat and dairy came from.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Contract farmers and rural neighbors of factory farms

how_it_helps.text: Bars new large concentrated animal feeding operations from starting or expanding, requires existing ones to cease operating as large CAFOs after January 1, 2041, and sets civil penalties of up to $10,000 per violation per day.

Creates a voluntary transition program funded at $10 billion per year that pays owners of animal feeding operations to pay off farm debt and convert their property to alternative agriculture, conditioned on a permanent easement barring the feeding operation.

Makes integrators — the meat companies that control contract farms — legally liable for dead animal and manure disposal, air and water pollution, harms to neighboring residents' health and property values, and harms to the contract growers themselves, with those duties nontransferable.

Requires large meatpackers to buy at least 50% of their daily slaughter volume through open spot-market sales from independent producers, restricts the forward contracts and formula prices that shift price risk onto farmers, and bans the poultry pay 'tournament system' when growers are ranked on factors outside their control.

Restores mandatory country-of-origin labeling for beef and pork, extends it to dairy products, and allows a 'Product of USA' label only on meat from animals exclusively born, raised, and slaughtered in the United States.

Gives USDA enforcement authority over live poultry dealers and awards attorney fees to growers who prevail in suits under the Packers and Stockyards Act, making it practical for individual farmers to sue.

analysis.who_pays: Large meatpacking companies and poultry integrators, which would face open-market buying mandates, new liability for farm pollution, and lost control over contract growers; owners of large factory farms, who would have to transition away or take the buyout; and taxpayers, who would fund the $10 billion annual transition program. Shoppers could face somewhat higher meat prices as the industry adjusted.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large meatpackers, integrators, and factory farm owners

drawbacks.text: The $10 billion annual price tag — roughly $100 billion over the decade — would come directly from the Treasury without an offsetting revenue source.
The mandatory 2041 shutdown deadline applies to all large CAFOs, not just those that decline transition grants, raising costs for compliant operators and potentially for consumers.

Requiring half of every large packer's daily slaughter to be bought through spot markets is a major intervention in how meat companies procure livestock; supporters see it as restoring price discovery for farmers, while critics argue it raises procurement costs and could nudge retail meat prices upward.

A previous mandatory country-of-origin labeling law for beef and pork was repealed in 2015 after trading partners won World Trade Organization rulings and imposed retaliatory tariffs, so restoring it carries a renewed risk of trade retaliation against U.S. exports.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits run to a broad, dispersed group — farmers facing concentrated buyers, rural residents breathing feedlot air, shoppers wanting honest labels — while the costs fall on a few very large companies and, in part, on taxpayers. The chief design weaknesses are the unfunded $10 billion annual appropriation and the blunt 2041 deadline, which a more targeted phase-out could have softened. On balance, the bill's purpose was to shift bargaining power and pollution costs from small farmers and rural communities to the largest firms in the meat business; the honest objection is not the goal but the cost and rigidity of the tools chosen.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee on February 2, 2023, and the committee never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Booker introduced the bill in the Senate on February 2, 2023, joined by Senators Warren and Sanders.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry the same day.
No further action was ever recorded: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action, through the end of the 118th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large meatpackers and poultry integrators are better off, since the open-market purchasing mandates, pollution liability, and grower protections never took effect. Owners of large factory farms also keep operating without a phase-out deadline. Contract growers and rural neighbors of factory farms remain under the pre-bill rules, in which pollution liability largely falls on growers and packers face no spot-market requirement.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no roll-call exists; all five Senate backers were Democrats or the independent Sanders, no Republican cosponsored, and the committee's Democratic majority did not advance it either.

industries.industry: Large meatpackers (beef, pork, and poultry processing)
industries.note: Packers would have to buy at least half of each day's slaughter through open competitive bidding, are barred from owning or feeding the livestock they slaughter, and integrators among them would become liable for farm pollution and harms to neighbors and growers. Their control over pricing and contract terms — the source of their profits — is what the bill targets.

industries.industry: Poultry integrators and live poultry dealers
industries.note: The bill bans the tournament pay system when growers are ranked on factors the company controls, requires disclosure of the data behind grower pay, limits retaliatory firings, and brings poultry dealers under USDA enforcement with attorney fees available to suing growers. These companies profit from contract structures that shift risk onto growers.

industries.industry: Large CAFO operators (industrial dairy, hog, cattle, and poultry feeding operations)
industries.note: No new large CAFOs could start or expand, and existing ones must cease operating as large CAFOs by 2041, with voluntary $10 billion-per-year grants to pay off debt and convert to other farming. Communities near these operations absorb manure runoff, odors, and property-value losses today.

industries.industry: Meat and dairy importers and integrated import brands
industries.note: Restored country-of-origin labeling and the exclusive 'Product of USA' standard would require imported product to be labeled by origin, reducing the value of foreign-raised beef and pork sold alongside domestic goods. Shoppers gain clearer information; importers gain nothing.

industries.industry: Independent livestock producers and contract growers
industries.note: These are the bill's intended beneficiaries: stronger price discovery, bargaining protections, liability shifted onto integrators, and a paid exit ramp from debt-laden feeding operations. They are small businesses, not a concentrated industry, which is part of why the bill struggled to move.
